(p-82) **Surat al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection)**

Its purpose is to demonstrate the greatness of the one clothed in garments (al-Muddaththir), who was commanded to warn, ﷺ, and the greatness of the One who sent him, glory be to Him, and the perfection of His power. He disclosed to him the sciences until they became realities after being mere traces, through the explanation at the end of its surah, that this Qur'an is a great reminder, because of the clarity of meanings, the sweetness of words, the majesty of its arrangements, the brilliance of its composition, and the loftiness of its aims, which He deposited in it [Allah -]. Therefore it is beloved to every disposition, and its hidden secrets and allusions are known through sincerity of intention and strength of resolve, to the extent that after it is unveiled and takes effect, it is as if it had been forgotten after being memorized. So remind: ﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 55], and so he memorizes it, knows its meanings, and takes on its character. The only thing that prevents this is the will of Allah, the Exalted. Whoever He wills, He veils it from him entirely and completely, and whoever He wills, He lifts the veil from him and makes it help him (p-83) upon the greatest correctness, without doubt or suspicion, and He reveals to him its intimate and bridal beauties, bestows upon him its jewels and precious things, and adorns him with it, so that it becomes his possession and his governor, just as al-Muddaththir ﷺ was when the Qur'an was his character. Its name, al-Qiyamah, is very clear in this, and there is nothing in it that establishes the indication of this except it, when the verse is contemplated, along with what it alludes to. The "la" is negating the oath or emphasizing it, and yet it is in clarity to a degree that does not need an oath [upon it -], because no one leaves under his hand those who transgress against one another, and who dispose of what he has entrusted to them without account. So how much more so the Most Wise of the wise, who appointed His servants, many times their number, from among the angels, who turn over every moment among them the cups of death, and take from them by His command, glory be to Him, to His abode of the barzakh in preparation for the gathering, driving them in groups after groups back to the earth until the assembly ends in the graves, and He gathers them by the blast in the trumpet (al-naqur), and the blowing into the horn (al-sur), to the courtyard of reckoning for reward and punishment. He did not veil the knowledge of this until most of creation went astray from it, except by His will, glory be to Him, through the dominance of the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah), until the self-reproaching soul (al-lawwamah) became immersed in evil, severely blaming itself for refraining from any of it. Likewise, what He revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, until it became his character, and to whoever of his followers He wills, except by His will, glory be to Him (p-84), through the dominance of the tranquil soul (al-mutma'innah), until all become pure spirit, [and -] unmixed, pure light.

(In the name of Allah) who ennobled His Messenger ﷺ and made the creation unable to match His Book, with the majesty that is His. (The Most Merciful) who encompassed the people of guidance and misguidance with the two blessings of origination and clarification. (The Most Compassionate) who singled out the people of care with rectitude in words and deeds.

* *

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the Hereafter at the beginning of the surah al-Muddaththir, and warned of it by the expression "al-naqur" and what followed it, then He repeated its matter at its end, and mentioned taqwa, which is the greatest means of success in it, and forgiveness, which is its greatest remedy. The disbelievers used to deny it, and He, glory be to Him, had established proofs for it from the beginning of the Qur'an until here, sometimes with an oath and sometimes without it, which made it a matter of self-evident truths. The custom had dictated that when the listener denies the one who informs him, the informant swears to what he told him. But swearing with the certainty of stubbornness is of no benefit. So He, glory be to Him, the Exalted, indicated that the matter had become independent of an oath, because of its manifestness, which none denies except a stubborn one. So He said, indicating its magnification and the emphasis on its matter by mentioning it and affirming its matter by not swearing or by emphasizing it: ﴿I do not swear﴾, meaning, I do not make the oath, or I make it emphatically, ﴿by the Day of Resurrection﴾, on the existence of the Day of Resurrection, or because of its existence, since the matter (p-85) is independent of that [from it -]. And according to the view that it is an oath, it is emphasized by the negative, and its inclusion in emphasis is permissible, indeed very common in their speech. It is permissible to swear by a thing with reference to its existence, to indicate that it is at the highest degree of greatness, as a person says: "By Allah, Allah exists," meaning: there is nothing I can swear by to establish its existence, O denier, that is greater than Him [until -] I swear by it, and I have no choice but to swear for your denial, so I swear by Him to it. Thus the meaning then is that there is nothing more indicative of the greatness of Allah than these two things, and therefore I make the oath by them. The secret of the emphasis [with "la" -], as al-Razi said in al-Lawami', is that affirmation by way of negation is more emphatic, as if He first rejected the denier and then affirmed the oath second, for combining negation and affirmation is a proof of restriction.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 75, verse 2:

Since it is established and known, and manifest to the utmost degree, that whoever is summoned by the King [to] account, reckoning [and reward] and punishment will blame himself for not having striven hard in doing what pleases the King, for sincerity in loyalty to Him, for inclining toward Him and keeping company with Him. The blaming of the self will be most prevalent on that Day. Its awareness of blame, which follows from awareness of universal and particular matters and from knowing good and evil and distinguishing between them, is among the greatest proofs of the perfect power of the Creator and the completeness of His greatness, which necessitates the bringing into being of that Day (p-86) to manifest His greatness, [His judgment] and His wisdom. He said: ﴿Nay, I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾, in accordance with what has passed concerning whether the *ba'* is a supplementary particle or indicates cause. *Al-lawwamah* means the soul that blames its owner, and it may be good or evil. The good soul becomes a cause of salvation on that Day, and the other [becomes] a cause of destruction. If it blames for evil or for neglecting good, it saves; if it blames for the opposite, it destroys. In any case it must blame, and it lies between *al-ammarah* (the soul that commands evil) and *al-mutma'innah* (the soul at peace), so whichever of these two predominates over it, it is within that category. Al-Razi said in *al-Lawami'*: The *mutma'innah* is the soul that submits to God's commands; the *ammarah* is the one opposed to it, following desire; and the *lawwamah* is the one that struggles, sometimes having the upper hand and sometimes being overpowered. It is the human soul specifically, because it lies between the stages of good and evil, perfection and deficiency, ascent and descent, obedience and disobedience. Al-Imam al-Suhrawardi said in the fifty-sixth chapter of his *Ma'arif*: It is one soul with differing attributes; the angels are at the degree of perfection, while the other animals are at the level of deficiency. For this reason He combined the Resurrection with the *lawwamah*, because reward and punishment apply to the human being and not to the angels (p-87) or to dumb animals. The blaming of the *lawwamah* will intensify on that Day over the absence of good or the failure to increase it. "I do not swear" by this [i.e., the Resurrection] regarding that, [since it is] among the clearest indications of His glory, may He be exalted, for the matter regarding that is too evident to need an oath.

When the implied meaning, which all that precedes points to, was the answer to the oath, namely, "Indeed you, by God, are truthful in your warning, so there must be a sounding in the *al-nāqūr* (the trumpet) through the blowing into the *al-ṣūr* (the horn)," [the author] proceeded, after alluding to the magnitude of the matter of the Resurrection through what the omission of the answer indicates, that it is a matter so clear and so certain to occur that it is hidden from no one. He rebukes whoever doubts it after this, saying: ﴿Does man suppose﴾, that is, this kind of creature who inclines toward self-companionship, looks to his own comfort, and rejoices in accordance with his own portion, and he attributed the verb to the whole species because most of them are like this, due to the dominance of desires over reason, except whom God has protected, ﴿that We shall not gather his bones﴾, that is, "that I", [i.e., that We will not gather].

Since among them are those who go to great lengths in denial, he also expressed it with the particle of emphasis, saying: "We shall not gather," meaning, with what We possess of greatness, ﴿his bones﴾, that is, those which are the framework of his body and its pillar, [made] from the earth, so that He would restore them as they were after they had been torn apart, crumbled, scattered, worn away, and effaced. The lightened form (*al-mukhaffafa*) has taken the place of the two objects of "yaḥsabu" (supposes), which are understood as "yaḥsabunā" (supposes us), not gathering [them].

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Since His statement had preceded, informing about the people of disbelief, ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 46], then there preceded at the beginning of the surah His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 8] up to His statement: ﴿a difficult day﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 10]. The meaning of this is the Day of Resurrection, and the threat concerning it is for the one mentioned afterward in His statement: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], and the verses that follow, and whoever was in his state of denying the occurrence of that Day. Then its mention was repeated when answering those who were asked: ﴿What led you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42]. So in this surah the discourse was expanded in explaining the mention of that Day and its terrors, and an allusion was made to the state of whoever denied it in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 6], and in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Does man suppose that We shall not gather his bones?﴾ Then He followed this with the mention of the conditions of creatures on that Day: ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]. [End of quotation.]

When he attributed the reckoning to the human kind (*nawʿ*), it was because some of them say, "We will not be resurrected, because we will crumble and be annihilated," he answered them, saying: ﴿Yes﴾, meaning: We will certainly gather his bones and assemble his parts, because We are capable of separating his bones and breaking them apart after they have been knotted together when he was a single drop (*nutfa*). For whoever is capable of separating is capable of gathering and joining, while We are ﴿capable﴾, meaning: by virtue of the greatness that is Ours, ﴿of [restoring] even﴾

Since levelling the small is more difficult, He said: ﴿We will level his fingertips (*banān*)﴾, meaning his fingers [or -] his phalanges (*sulāmiyyāt*), which are the small bones in his hands and feet, each of which is the length of a finger or less. He singled them out because they are the extremities of the body and the last thing by which his creation is completed, by joining some of them to others as they were before death, in the same way. The large bones (p. 89) are included by way of greater priority, because they are more evident. There is no difference between our levelling of those from the drop and our levelling of him from the dust, for it [the body] cannot be levelled while it is the mould of the body except by levelling what is upon it of the garment of flesh, sinew and skin, as the one who knows it recognises it. Thus the levelling of the fingertips is a *kināya* (metonymy) for the levelling of the whole structure, just as if it were said to you, "Can you assemble this colocynth (*ḥanẓal*)?" and you said, "Yes," and [can you assemble] the mustard seed (*khardal*), together with what is understood from singling them out as a reminder of the marvellous craftsmanship in them, from which flow the subtle benefits they possess. Or [it means]: We will level them now, gathering them into the state they were in as a drop, from the joining before their separation and dispersal, until they become like the sole of a camel's foot. For the One who is capable of separating the fingertips so that they are prepared for delicate works is capable of gathering them, whereupon that benefit departs from them. Whoever is capable of separating water after its mixing and gathering it after its separation is capable of gathering dust after its dispersal. In any case, this is a reminder to reflect upon the subtlety of the separation of the fingertips and the marvellous workmanship in them, which necessitates certainty that their Maker is capable of everything He wills.

In the *Qāmūs* (al-Fīrūzābādī) it says: *banān*: the fingers, or their tips. *Sulāmā* (on the pattern of *ḥubārā*): small bones the length of a finger or less in the hand and foot.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 5:**

When what had been mentioned earlier, which indicated that the Resurrection is in the utmost degree of manifestness, had preceded, he turned away from this denial and said, building upon what its implied sense is: he does not reckon the non-existence of that, because it is of such manifestness that it does not need great reflection; so if he followed his intellect, he would recognize the truth. ﴿Rather, man wishes﴾, i.e., brings about the wish, ﴿man﴾. The noun is stated in the place of the pronoun to make explicit the generality, in accordance with the disposition of nature, which requires that he not reflect on the Hereafter despite its great manifestness, because he is preoccupied with his desires; so there is no salvation except by the protection of Allah, exalted is He. The object of "wishes" is omitted to indicate that everything he wishes according to the requirement of his nature and desires is beyond its proper bounds, and for it he is held accountable, because he is a servant, and the servant must be mindful of his master, wishing only what He commands him to. When he wishes what He has commanded him, the wish is not attributed to him; rather, the wish belongs to the Master, not to him.

When that was the case, and his wish outside the command was disobedience, he said, giving the reason: ﴿so that he may commit wickedness before him﴾, i.e., the wish arises from him so that wickedness may occur from him in the future of his life, by fulfilling his desires and proceeding with his head held high in his caprice. His deceitful soul presents to him wishful hopes, widens for him the scope of expectation, and makes him covet forgiveness without works. Al-Hasan said: "You do not see the believer except blaming himself [and saying: What did I intend by my speech? What did I intend by my eating?], whereas the wicked one proceeds forward, not calling himself to account nor reproaching it." It is also permissible that the pronoun refer back to Allah, exalted is He, so that the meaning is: that he may perform wickedness [in the presence of] Allah, exalted is He, (p-91) and within His sight and hearing, while hoping that He will not hold him to account for it or requite him for his wickedness. He said in al-Qamus: "al-Fajr: the rushing forth into sins, and fornication, like al-Fujur."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 6:

Since he was deeply immersed in this attribute, it produced in him mockery of this great matter, so he expressed that by his saying: ﴿He asks﴾ [i.e.] a question of mockery and disbelief, and in the place of the object of "yas'alu" (he asks) a nominal clause is placed, consisting of a predicate placed first and a subject placed last. So he said: ﴿When⁠ [i.e.] at what time⁠ will be﴾ ﴿the Day of Resurrection⁠?﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 7:

When the answer was [the Day of ...] will be such-and-such, he turned away from it to what results from their deeming it unlikely, because it is more terrifying. So He said, indicating the ruin of the world through the stripping of man from his dwelling and from what he was accustomed to of his conditions, which makes it more terrifying, expressing it with the particle of certainty because it is its proper place: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾, meaning it becomes fixed, standing still, not blinking from the terror of what it sees. This is according to the reading of Nafi' with the fatha, and it points to the beginning of his state. The reading of the majority with the kasra points to its outcome, for its meaning is: bewildered, astonished and overwhelmed, from baraqa al-rajul (the man was dazzled), when he looks at lightning and his sight is dimmed and scattered, like the scattering of a thing in liquid when its container is opened. This is supported by the reading of baliqa, from baliqa al-bab (the door was opened), and balaqa al-bab, like nasara, means he opened it entirely; or, intensively, abalqahu fa-inbalaq; and baliqa, like fariha, means he was bewildered. So said the Qamus.

When the signs of the heavens were more fearsome, He mentioned them, beginning with that which cold had imprinted, as an indication of the intensity of heat, blazing, and the seizing of breaths, which necessitates extreme despair. So He said: ﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾. That is, it found its eclipse, in that Allah the Exalted eclipsed it, removing its form entirely, just as the form of an eclipsed earth is removed. This is by removing its light, without a cause, because in that Day the linkage of causes to their effects is dissolved, and extraordinary events (khawāriq, breaches of ordinary custom) appear, as is shown by His saying:

﴿And the sun and the moon are joined﴾, that is, a gathering of the utmost firmness and intensity, as the masculine form (التَّذْكِيرُ, tadhkīr, masculine gender) implies, [و -] in the easiest and most facile manner. ﴿The sun﴾, that is, the sign of the day, ﴿and the moon﴾, despite its not giving light, although its light now comes from the sun's light. Benefit from both is lost, and with the going of light and the scattering of sight, both are perceived, because there is complete unveiling of the hidden things, as He, exalted, said: ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, so your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22]. After their gathering, they are cast into the Fire, as if they were two bulls with their legs hamstrung (ثَوْرانِ عَقِيرانِ). The verb is cast in the passive form because the awe lies in the bare fact of their being gathered, which takes them out of the ordinary course, and to indicate ease.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 10:

When the matter of the Resurrection had been magnified by what preceded, he emphasized this by saying that the matter on that Day is other than what we are accustomed to in this world, namely finding a fugitive, or a judge other than the one the wanted person fears, or anything of the scattering and dispersal of the gathering. Thus He said: ﴿The human being will say﴾, that is, out of the intensity of his terror, following his natural inclination, ﴿on that day﴾, that is, when this momentous affair and this greatest calamity has come. He related "yaqulu" (he says) with a nominal sentence consisting of a predicate placed first and a subject placed last, and so he said: ﴿Where is the escape?﴾, that is, where is the fleeing, the place to which one flees, and the time that is suitable for that. It is the saying of one in despair and bewilderment, which his natural disposition has driven him to, and that is when Hell is led forth with seventy thousand chains, each chain held by seventy thousand angels, and it has a roaring and a shrieking.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 11:

When that day comes, the day when all means are severed, He says, negating what was asked about, using the particle of deterrence: ﴿Kallā﴾ (No!), meaning: this should not be said, for there is no way for its meaning to exist, and that meaning is ﴿lā wazar﴾ (there is no refuge), that is, no shelter or place of safeguard, no fortress, no place of seeking refuge or protection. That this is said as the speech of man, a return from his natural disposition to his intellect, is more fitting and more indicative of the terror, because he understands that after asking about the great terror, he considered the whole matter and realized that there is no stratagem in any way at all, so he said, expressing it with the particle that gathers all the aspects of deterrence.

Since the meaning is: there is no refuge from Allah except unto Him, because His dominion encompasses all and His power is comprehensive, He said, conveying this on His behalf and mentioning the attribute of beneficence, as a rebuke to the self for its lack of gratitude: ﴿To your Lord﴾, that is, the One who has bestowed upon you every kind of favour, alone, not (p-94) to anything other than Him. ﴿On that Day﴾, that is, when these things are [the case]: ﴿the place of rest﴾, that is, the resting-place of all creation [all of them] — those who speak and those who are silent — and the place of their rest and its time, is unto His judgment, glory be to Him, and His will, outwardly and inwardly, with no judgment [belonging] to anyone other than Him in any respect, whether outward or inward, as it is in this world.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 13:

When the question concerning the cause of this settling arose, he said, resuming, building the verb in the passive voice because what is disclosed is the act of uncovering the secrets, not who the uncoverer is, and to indicate how easy that is for Him, glorified and exalted be He, since whoever He commissions to do it, his doing is possible whoever he may be: ﴿He will be informed﴾, that is, he will be told with a great, thorough informing, ﴿man, on that day﴾ [that is,] when this greatest quaking takes place, ﴿of what he sent forward﴾, that is, of his great deeds, ﴿and put off﴾, that is, at the beginning and end of his life, as a metaphor for thoroughness; or, of what he sent forward by giving precedence to it over other things, whether it was the Law or desire; or, of what he did during the span of his life, and of what he put off, meaning the deed he was prevented from doing by death overtaking him, so that he will be informed of what he used to do in his hopes, had his term been extended. Or, what he sent forward is what he did himself, and what he put off is what he established as a precedent, so that people acted upon it after him, whether good or evil. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and al-Ghazali followed this view in the third chapter of the Book of Sales in the Ihya'.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 14:

When the Resurrection was magnified by the disclosure of its secrets and the reporting of it, and it is the case that a person is only informed of what he is ignorant of or absent from, and [it is] that forgetting is something that comes lightly to a person in this world, and that Day is the Day of the removal of the veil, it was increased in magnitude by the announcement that it will make clear the insight of the person, until he becomes present to all that pertains to him. The sense, then, is: he is not ignorant of any of that, nor in need of being informed of it. He said, building upon this: ﴿Nay, man [each one of this kind] against himself﴾ specifically, ﴿is a clear insight﴾, that is, a clear proof against his deeds. The ta' (of baṣīrah) is for emphasis (mubālaghah). He means that he is at the utmost of knowledge of the states of his own self, for when he reflects and looks closely, and does not stop at his appetites, he recognizes the good of his deed from its bad. As for the world, that is because the primordial natures (al-fiṭar al-ūlā) bear witness to good and evil, as he ﷺ indicated by his saying: "Righteousness is that to which the soul is at rest and the heart is at ease, and sin is that which stirs in the breast and the soul is uneasy about, even if people give you legal opinions and give you opinions." Narrated by Imam Aḥmad from Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī (may Allah be pleased with him). And his ﷺ saying: "Among what people have gained from the words of the first prophethood is: if you have no shame, then do what you wish." Narrated by al-Bukhari from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him). As for the Hereafter, Allah gives him on that Day the power of remembrance, until all his deeds are before his eyes, for He, exalted is He, removes from him the bodily distractions and uncovers from him the soul's veils, until his deeds become represented to him as though he sees them, and his excuse does not benefit him, because every excuse he offers for himself is known to be false by the very fact of its existence, not by anything external to it. Sometimes his Creator has brought him into being upon knowledge and soundness of the means that remove causes, and sometimes by making his limbs speak.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 15:

Since man, on that Day, will offer excuses for all his evil deeds and dispute with the utmost vehemence, and since the one who disputes usually [thinks] that he has not sinned, or does not know of any sin of his, He said: ﴿Even if he should put forth his excuses﴾ — that is, he mentions them with the utmost speed, without stammering, indicating the utmost sincerity, earnestness and flattery — ﴿his excuses﴾, that is, every speech by which he can hope to be freed. It is the plural of ʿudhr (excuse) or maʿdhira (plea), which is the exertion of stratagem in warding off a defect. In al-Qamus (the dictionary) it is said: al-maʿadhir (excuses) means "veils" and "proofs," the plural of miʿdhar, because the two share the general meaning of covering: with a fatḥah, "covering," and with a kasrah, "concealing the sinner." And a proof (ḥujjah) is for covering a sin. So the meaning is that he is a proof against himself, even if he argues on its behalf and strives to conceal its faults, and so excuses will not be accepted from him, because he was given insight but blinded it through the subjugation of the self and its desires. That insight is the light of knowledge established in the primordial nature (fiṭrah). It is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The excuse of the wrongdoers will not benefit them﴾ [Ghafir: 52].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 16:

Since the whole meaning of this is that the human being is veiled in this abode from perceiving the realities, by what is in him of appetites, laziness and sluggishness, because of his deficiencies, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) was free of all that, because Allah created him perfect, and His elevating him after his birth each day through the stages of perfection, until he reached a degree where nothing preoccupied him [from the sciences -], so that he was such that he saw the places of trials within the houses as one sees the places of rain, and saw behind him as he saw in front of him, and he would say: "By Allah, your humility and your bowing are not hidden from me; indeed I see you from behind my back." The Prophet (ﷺ) would see in the deepest darkness and in other things, by reason of the subtlety of his substance (that no one other than him attained), and this indicates complete unveiling. But he [was -] (p-98) (ﷺ), out of his exalting of this Qur'an, because of the majesty it has in itself, and because of what it contains of treasures of happiness and sciences which have no limit, so that they cannot be exhausted, and because it is the speech of the Most Great King, sent down by His command to him (ﷺ) through His messenger Jibril (peace be upon him), he would experience intense difficulty upon hearing it at the first of its coming. So he would move his tongue with it, hastening to take care to memorize it, so that nothing of it would escape him. Allah, glorified is He, had concluded what preceded it with excuses, and hastening was among what one apologizes for. What drives every act that calls for blame and apology is the innate love of the immediate that man is created with. Allah, glorified is He, said, as a result of these premises, which necessitate the unveiling of things to the human being, which necessitates informing him of them and fearing their consequences, so that he does not incline toward the immediate and does not fall into disobedience: were it not for what He occupied him with of veiling, informing that He, glorified and exalted is He, has removed from the Prophet (ﷺ) those veils and brought him from the rank of "Had the veil been removed, I would not have increased in certainty" to its utmost end; and that He is capable of what He wills of unveiling what He wills to whom He wills, just as He unveils to every person his deeds on the Day of Resurrection, until he comes to know what he sent forward of them and what he delayed; and as an admonition that he (ﷺ) has no acquisition in this Qur'an (p-99) except by good receiving, distancing it from the speech of humans, and as a preparation by what moves his tongue with the Qur'an before the completion of the delivery, to censure what the human being is created with: ﴿Do not move with it﴾, that is, the Qur'an, which is a reminder; whoever wills may remember it, were it not for the veil of the Will. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has unveiled the veil of the Will for this noble Prophet (ﷺ), and willed that he should remember it, when He said ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30], because He did not send it down to him except through his acquisition, and he had willed that. ﴿Your tongue﴾, which has no movement except in the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He.

Since this movement had no benefit, given Allah's preservation of it for him in every state, except seeking obedience through haste, and haste is doing a thing before its most fitting time, although the Prophet (ﷺ) is rewarded for that with the greatest reward, because nothing drives him to it except the love of Allah and the love of what comes from Him, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made it a cause even though it was not intended, and said: ﴿that you may hasten with it﴾, meaning, by carrying it and taking it before Jibril, Our messenger, finishes delivering it to you, out of fear that it might slip away from you. This is because this haste, although it is among the perfections in relation to you and to your brothers among the prophets (peace be upon them), as Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84], (p-100) is from the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwama), which blames for neglecting to hasten to acts of good; so other acts of the soul at rest (al-nafs al-mutma'inna) are more perfect than it. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) moved from a complete station to one more complete than it. This speech concerning the Qur'an, and what follows it, was a distinction between the two attributes of the self-reproaching soul: in good and in evil. The verse refers to His saying, in al-Muddaththir, as a quotation: ﴿This is but the speech of a human﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25], and what lies between them is a digression describing the state of the Resurrection, which was brought about by His saying ﴿I will drive him into Saqar﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26]. That is, what deluded the one who fabricated against the Qur'an consisted of two matters: one, that it is magic, and the other, that it is the speech of a human. Certain knowledge is established of the negation of the first. As for the second, the Prophet (ﷺ) feared that he might not perfect its memorization, so that a word might enter it, for example, and it would then be the speech of a human. So Allah, exalted is He, forbade him from hastening and guaranteed him its preservation. Then He gave the reason for this prohibition in His saying, emphasizing it because it is among its implications:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, upon Us﴾, i.e., by what We possess of greatness, not upon anyone other than Us, ﴿is its collection﴾, i.e., in your breast, so that We establish it and preserve it, ﴿and its recitation﴾, i.e., the releasing of your tongue with it and its establishment in its rank within the Book, in the state of it being collected in the most complete collection, facilitated in the finest facilitation. So ease your soul of what you have endured concerning the matter of hardship and what you suffer of toil.

(p-101) When He forbade him, He then commanded him, saying: ﴿So when We have recited it﴾, i.e., when We empowered Jibril, upon him be peace, to convey it to you, just as We bore it to him, by what We have of greatness and in accordance with it, ﴿then follow﴾, i.e., with the utmost of your effort, by giving ear and presence of mind, ﴿its recitation﴾, i.e., its reading, gathered according to the way our Messenger conveyed it to you, and We gathered it for you in your breast. Repeat its recitation until it becomes for you a great faculty, and act upon it until it becomes for you a disposition, so that it will be your guide to every good. Thus the pronoun may refer to the Qur'an, with "the Qur'an" here meaning the recitation, which he expressed by it as a magnification of it, i.e., follow the recitation of the Qur'an, that is, the recitation of Jibril, upon him be peace. Had it been on its ordinary usage, it would not have been objectionable, since what is intended by it is particular while the pronoun is general. And the pronoun may refer to Jibril, upon him be peace, i.e., follow his recitation and do not contend with him.

Since the explanation of its words and arrangement, in whatever manner he heard them, such as the sound of a bell (ṣalṣalat al-jaras) and other sounds, and the explanation of its meanings and the treasures of knowledge it contains, with a greatness beyond what description can reach, He indicated this with the particle of delay (adāt al-tarākhī), so He said, showing that the delay of explanation from the time of address to the time of need is permissible, and implying that he would hasten to ask about the meaning just as he would hasten to recite: ﴿Then﴾. He emphasized this, indicating that because of its greatness it is something that requires pausing over, so He said: ﴿Indeed, upon Us﴾ (p-102), that is, by the greatness that We possess, ﴿its clarification﴾, that is, the clarification of its words and meanings for you, whether you heard it from Jibril (peace be upon him) with a sound like the ringing of a bell, or in the ordinary speech of people with voice and letters, and for others through your tongue and the tongues of the scholars of your community. [And the verse] points to abandoning hastiness altogether, for if He forbade it in the greatest and most important matters, then others are forbidden by way of greater necessity. Al-Bukhari narrated in the tafsir (exegesis) of this verse, at the beginning and end of his Ṣaḥīḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to struggle with the revelation with great difficulty, and he would move his lips." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "So I move them for you as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to move them." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed the verse, up to His saying: "Collect it in your breast and then recite it," ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾. He said: "So listen to it and be attentive. Then indeed upon Us is its recitation." He said: "So whenever Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen with lowered head, and when Jibril (peace be upon him) departed, the Prophet (ﷺ) would recite it just as Jibril (peace be upon him) had recited it to him," as Allah had promised him the safeguarding of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord; and He encompasses what is with them and has enumerated everything in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

[p-103] Since Glorified and Exalted is He had concluded the discourse about the deniers by stating that their deeds are preserved, and that every person is a witness against himself, for he knows the good and the evil of what he does even if he offers excuses, and were it not for this, his connection to it would not be so strong, and He concluded with the guarantee of the clarity of the Qur'an, so it became a clear witness over every human being through its great clarity, He said, negating what might be supposed of their ignorance of the ugliness of their deeds, which their excuse-making implies, indicating that the human being is naturally inclined to haste, after the prohibition against haste in the most precious, highest, most important and most fitting matters, because it is the foundation of religion, so that this would reinforce the prohibition against haste in the Qur'an, and reinforce their reproach for loving the fleeting, intensifying their rebuke for following their nature and abandoning what knowledge and reason require: ﴿No!﴾, meaning none of them is ignorant of the ugliness of what they committed, even if they make excuses, and none of them committed any of it out of ignorance. ﴿Rather﴾ they ﴿love﴾, meaning a love that is renewed and continuous through the renewal of time, ﴿the fleeting﴾, as evidenced by their turning to it with the utmost turning and taking it. Their love for it necessitated for them the commission of what they know to be ugly, for the Hereafter and this world are two co-wives; whoever loves one of them will inevitably do what distances him from the other. For "Your love for a thing blinds you and deafens you." This is unlike our Prophet (ﷺ) in regard to haste in general, let alone the fleeting. Rather, We created him upon perfection, so he would strive with great intensity in recitation to overcome haste. When We forbade him from that, he ceased, returning to his perfect nature, which is not tainted by any deficiency. Likewise his command was by creation, with no reluctance accompanying it and no strain, for his tranquil soul was the dominant one and held the greatest authority. And because of the harm to both abodes and because they love the fleeting, He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 21:

﴿And you leave﴾: that is, they abandon [it] in whatever manner it may be, even though it is not commendable. ﴿the Hereafter﴾: because they hate it, due to their committing what will harm them therein. He used the plural pronoun, although the address is directed to the human being, out of regard for the meaning, indicating that he is not spared from the blameworthy haste [except -] individuals whom Allah protected by His overwhelming power. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (interlocking omission): He mentioned love first as a proof of hatred second, and abandonment second as a proof of turning toward and taking first. Thus their self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah) blames them for falling short in evil, just as your soul urges you to increase in good and to hasten toward it, so excellent is the soul that it is, and so may you raise its station. As for their souls, they urge them, for the sake of blame, to fall short in evil, to incline toward the hasty, perishing [world], and to renounce the lasting [world] because it is absent; so wretched are the souls that they are.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 22:

When he mentioned the Hereafter, which they had turned away from, he mentioned what will happen in it, making clear their ignorance, foolishness and lack of intellect, as a warning to those who turn their backs on it and an encouragement to those who turn toward it, out of gentleness toward them and mercy for them. So He said: ﴿Faces﴾, that is, of those who are gathered (al-mahshurin), and they are all of creation, ﴿on that Day﴾, that is, when the Resurrection occurs, ﴿radiant﴾ from (p-105) al-nadra (radiance) with the letter ḍād, which is blessing and well-being; that is, they are bright and shining, with the traces of blessing visible upon them, such that this indicates the blessedness of their owners.

﴿إلى رَبِّها﴾ means toward the one who bestows (grace) upon them specifically, in that looking at anything else is considered as not looking at all. ﴿ناظِرَةٌ﴾ means that they are always fixing their eyes toward His generosity through self-disclosure (tajalli), with no heedlessness toward that. When He removes the veil from them, they see Him with their eyes, as evidenced by the transitive use of "ilā" (to). That is seeing openly, without being hidden, pressed, or crowded, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), most of the exegetes (mufassirun), and all the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the adherents of the prophetic tradition) have said. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) in authentic hadiths through many chains, to the extent that it is widely known, and the seeing is as is illustrated in the hadiths:

"As the moon is seen on the night of the full moon." Each one who wants to see it does so from his house, being alone with it. This is the point of comparison, not that He is in a direction or in a state that has a likeness. Exalted is Allah above likeness. Likewise is the seeing of the Prophet (ﷺ) in dreams by many persons in distant lands at the same time. He placed the preposition (al-jarr), which indicates exclusivity, first, as a sign that this seeing is distinct from looking at anything else, so it is not considered seeing in relation to other things. It also indicates that those faces are absorbed in contemplating His beauty, such that they never slacken from that, and their gaze does not count anything else as worthy. They are safe from (p-106) having a calamity inflicted upon them (﴿تَظُنُّ أَن يُفْعَلَ بِهَا فَاقِرَةٌ﴾). He expressed (the meaning) by "faces" to refer to their possessors, because faces are the clearest indicator of joy, and so that mentioning them would be more explicit that the intended meaning of seeing is its literal reality. He made it even more explicit by the transitive use of "ilā," since "intizār" (waiting) is not transitive with it.

The Imam, Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him), said in the Book of Love in the Ihya' (Revival of the Religious Sciences), after permitting that Allah may create the seeing in a direction or otherwise: "The truth is what has become evident to the People of the Sunnah and the community from the evidences of the Law, that this (seeing) is created in the eye, so that the word 'ru'ya' (seeing), 'nazar' (looking), and the other words used in the Law take their apparent meaning, since it is not permissible to abandon apparent meanings except out of necessity." End of quote.

The people of Paradise differ in their looking. It has been narrated that among them are those who look at Allah morning and evening. In another report: "Between the people and their looking at their Lord there is nothing but the cloak of majesty over His face in the Garden of Eden." They also differ in the degree of unveiling in beauty, intimacy, and delight, from which pleasure arises, according to their deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 24:

When he had mentioned the people of blessing, he followed them with their opposites, the people of retribution, saying: ﴿And faces on that Day﴾, meaning on that very day, ﴿will be scowling﴾, meaning intensely gloomy, frowning, and averse, because of the distress they are in, as though they had been submerged in it and sunk, after their conditions had been thoroughly tested and no way of escape had appeared to them.

The word *al-bāsil* (the one who is grim-faced in fierce battle) is more eloquent than *al-bāsir* (scowling), but it became predominantly applied to the brave, because of the intensity of the grimacing of his face at the clash of combat. And those faces are veiled from their Lord, and are looking toward the various kinds of punishment.

Since the expectation of harm is enough to produce caution against it and to make one exaggerate in using whatever protects from it, He said, indicating that He expressed by the face (wajh) the whole person: ﴿Expecting﴾, that is, anticipating, from what they see of the signs: ﴿that there will be done﴾ — He made it passive because the feared thing is the occurrence of harm, not its being from a specific agent — ﴿to them﴾, that is, to them, for when the face, which is the most noble part of the whole person, is struck, what is other than it is more deserving [of being struck]. ﴿A backbreaking calamity﴾, that is, a catastrophe that breaks the spine (faqar), which is the bone of the vertebral column, the hardest of the bones, so it becomes a calamity that breaks the back. Thus the verse is of the type of ihtibak (interlocking omission): mentioning the looking in the first clause is evidence of its opposite in the second, and mentioning the backbreaking calamity in the second clause is evidence of its opposite in the first.

When he described their love for the fleeting (worldly life) using the present tense, which indicates renewal and continuity, it implied that the love of anything else is entirely free of renewal. He then informed them that the soul will be cut off from the terror of the moment of ascent [with -], which indicates complete power, and that its decree cannot be turned back. So He said, deterring those who think this love will not cease: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning this love will not last. Rather, it must come to an end, and a very ugly end at that.

Since the one who loves the world is the soul (nafs), He left it implicit for that reason and because the context indicates it. So He said, mentioning the time-clause of what the particle of deterrence conveyed, whose implied sense is the absence of love: ﴿when it reaches﴾, meaning the soul turned toward the fleeting, with a matter that is certain (what the particle of certainty conveyed), ﴿the collarbones﴾, meaning the large bones of the upper chest. The singular is tarqwa (collarbone), the bones around the windpipe on the right and left of the notch of the throat, between the notch and the shoulder. Every person has two, and this is the place of the death rattle. Perhaps the dual was made plural to indicate how widely they spread with the greatest effort because of the distress the soul is in, since they gather from the far parts of the body to that place, and the space around them is constricted, as if the soul wants to leave by the nearest point to it. This is a kinaya (allusion) for being near death.

How excellent is the saying of Hatim al-Ta'i, and how closely it fits what is being discussed here regarding the matter of the soul:

Māwiyya, wealth does not avail a man
when on a day his breath rattles and his chest constricts.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 27:

When the people of the dying man become increasingly distressed at that time, and their searching for whatever could save the one near death intensifies, without it benefiting them in any way, their saying becomes as though no one specific were saying it. Therefore the verb ﴿وقِيلَ﴾ (and it is said) is put in the passive form, meaning: from every speaker to whom the dying man is dear, as a question expressing disbelief (istib'ad): ﴿مَن راقٍ﴾ (Who is a reciter?), that is: who is the one characterized by firm mastery in the matter of healing incantations (ruqa, the recitation of cures), so that he may recite over him and rescue him from what he is in, for he has reached a state in which no medicine is of any use, so there is no hope except in incantations. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that this saying is from some of the angels, asking about who will ascend with his soul to heaven: are they angels of mercy or angels of punishment? The first is the active participle of raqa, yarqa, meaning "to recite incantations" (ruqyah, with a fatha in the past tense and a kasra in the present), and the second, which means "to ascend," is with a kasra in the past tense and a kasra in the present. [The second, meaning "to ascend," is with a kasra in the past tense and a kasra in the present. -]

Since man is naturally disposed to lean toward one of the possible matters, he inclines to whatever he is most attached to by the nature of familiarity and the intensity of his adherence to what he is accustomed to, even by the slightest thing, He expressed by what is fit to be realized through conjecture, so He said: ﴿And he thinks﴾, i.e., the dying person, regarding what has appeared to him of the matters of the Hereafter, or the one who said "Is there anyone who can cure him?" from among his family; ﴿that it﴾, i.e., the great affair in which he [is -] ﴿is parting﴾, i.e., since in it there is what is loved of the worldly life, which is the greatest parting, the like of which there is no parting. Thus, in a report it is said that the servant struggles with the anguish of death and its agonies, and that his joints greet one another, [and] he says: "Peace be upon you. You are parting from me and I am parting from you until the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 29:

﴿And the shin shall be wound around the shin﴾ — i.e., this kind (of ordeal) is joined to the (other) shin; it is conjoined to it and attached to it, and one of the two turns around the other, so that they become like a single thing. It is a metaphor (kinaya) for death, because walking is not possible except with one of the two legs separated from the other. Or (it is a metaphor) for the extreme intensification of the matter and its nearness to deliverance being far off. The Arabs do not mention the shin in this context except in a grave matter, as in the phrase "he rolled up his shin" (shammara 'an saq), and when the fighting of those at war intensifies: "the markets drew close to one another" (danati al-suwq ba'duha min ba'd). So there is no separation except through the death of one of them, or something worse than his death, such as his defeat.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is a metaphor for the mingling of the severity of the last of this world with the severity of the first of the Hereafter. The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted, its implied sense being: his attachment to the world, his love for it, and his turning away from the Hereafter, will have ceased.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 30:

When He depicted the time of his (the disbeliever's) regret over the world and his turning away from it, He mentioned the ultimate end of that, saying, addressing the Prophet ﷺ alone with the address, as an indication that no one other than him understands this as it truly should be understood: ﴿To your Lord﴾, that is, the destination and the judgment of the One who did good to you by sending you and confirming you in all that you conveyed from Him, and who gave you victory over everyone who opposed you, not to anyone else. ﴿On that Day﴾, that is, when this matter occurs, ﴿the driving﴾ [i.e., the driving-along (al-suq) -] and the place of driving and its time, all of this is included in His judgment, while the rulings of the people of this world have been cut off from him. So either the angels will drive him to clear felicity, or to clear wretchedness. Or it is a metaphor for his being presented before God Most High after death, so that when the admonition about death is realized for him, his saying "Let me die so that I may rest" will not benefit him, for he returns through death to his master. If he was obedient, he will meet Him with what pleases Him, and if he was disobedient, he will meet Him with what a runaway slave meets with, in proportion to his running away.

When he mentioned his aversion to the Hereafter, he mentioned that its cause was his corrupting what God had given him of the faculties of knowledge and action, by leaving them idle from good and employing them in evil. So He said, explaining the deed of the obedient servant and the runaway, and conjoining it to ﴿He asks when the Day of Resurrection will be﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 6], whose meaning is denying the resurrection: ﴿So he neither affirmed nor prayed﴾. That is, this human being [about whom the discourse is] did not affirm the Messenger in what he reported regarding the evil deeds he used to do, nor did his faith lead him to spend in the paths of good to which he was urged, whether obligatory or recommended. The object was omitted because that is more far-reaching in generality.

When He mentioned the root of the religion (asl al-din), He followed it with its branches (furu', the subsidiary practices), indicating that the disbeliever is addressed by them as well. So He said: ﴿nor did he pray﴾, that is, what he was commanded to do of obligatory and other acts, so he did not hold fast to the rope of the Creator, nor did he reach the rope of the creatures in the manner that He legislated ma.

But he denied and turned away. (That is, he did the opposite of affirming the truth, by denying what Allah had brought to him; and he turned away, that is, he did the opposite of prayer, which is the bond between the created being and the Creator. He strove to act contrary to what his primordial, upright nature called him to, namely turning away from obedience, including prayer and other acts, until this became his habit, so that obedience no longer came to his mind after that, because the original nature had died and the commanding soul that inclines to evil had come alive. This is not a repetition, for the absence of affirmation does not necessarily entail denial.)

Since persisting in this (denial) is a great matter, far-removed that anyone would do it, how much more so would be to take pride in it and act arrogantly on its account, He pointed to it with the particle of distance, saying, indicating that the state regarding denial is arrogance, and what drives one to arrogance is affluence (al-taraf), and the cause of that is, first, submission together with the seal (al-tab') in corrupting the two faculties: the practical (al-'amaliyyah) and the cognitive (al-'ilmiyyah), until this bad disposition arises from them, namely indifference (ʿadam al-mubalah). That condition continued with him until it became a firm trait (malakah) in which he takes pride. ﴿Then he went﴾, that is, this person, after turning away from the truth, ﴿to his family﴾, not reflecting on the outcome of what he had done of denial [while being -] ﴿swaggering﴾, that is, taking pride in his denial, his turning away, and his indifference to that. It derives from al-matt (stretching). He replaced the second letter with an alif for lightness, so it became from al-matiyy, which is the back, as if he were helping himself to stretch his strides. Or, the strutting man, when he walks, bends his back. He did this only because of his boldness in disobedience, in place of shame, modesty and humility.

Since this is the extreme of wickedness, and people's family usually welcome such a person when he approaches them, especially when he is in this state among most people, He informed (him) of what is truly fitting to be said to him in place of "a greeting to his family," namely a great threat. So He said: ﴿Woe to you﴾, meaning: may Allah bring upon you what you dislike. The lam (al-lam, the emphatic particle) entered for extra emphasis and specification. The emphasis was increased by His saying: ﴿Then woe﴾, meaning: may Allah afflict you with one calamity after another. This emphasis conveys, in its intensity, an indication that he deserves it throughout the ages. So He said, using the particle of delay (thumma-like "then" in tara'i) to indicate the magnitude of what he committed and the strength of his deserving this emphasis:

﴿Then woe to you﴾, meaning, O you who have placed yourself in heedlessness below the station of the animals. ﴿Woe upon woe﴾, meaning, you have arrived at this ruin through a calamity that follows you, sometimes in quick succession and sometimes after a delay, some of it greater than the rest. That will certainly befall you, for this is a supplication from the One in whose hand is all affairs. It is also possible that (p-١١٤) the meaning is: woe to you for leaving what you are upon and turning to what benefits you. Ibn Jarir said in his commentary on al-Muddaththir: "When Abu Jahl mocked the guardians of the Fire being nineteen, Allah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ that he should go to him, take him by the hand in the valley of Makkah, and say to him: 'Woe to you, and again woe to you,' until the end of it. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that, Abu Jahl said: 'By Allah, neither you nor your Lord will do anything.' So Allah [-] disgraced him on the day of Badr." The end. It is possible to apply the four words to his four states: life, then death, then resurrection, then entry into the Fire. The meaning would then be: for you is the hateful now, and at death, resurrection, and entry into the Fire. Al-Baghawi said: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "Every nation has a Pharaoh, and the Pharaoh of this nation is Abu Jahl." The verse has also conveyed that whoever sets right the two faculties of his knowledge and his action, by believing in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and turns in repentance and establishes the prayer, then all the deeds that are its pillars follow it, and from that arises a good disposition, which is awe together with obedience. At that point it is said to him: ﴿Good news for you﴾, then good news, then good news [for you] , then good news.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 36:

When this was the conduct of one who has turned away from Allah altogether, so that no thought of His greatness has crossed his mind, he came to suppose that he is left unattended, that he has no owner, and that he himself is the lord (al-sayyid) with no servitude incumbent upon him; therefore he is not commanded or forbidden, and does not act except in accordance with his desires. He said, rebuking him and expressing it with "ḥusbān" (supposing), the impulse behind which is deficiency of intellect: ﴿Does man suppose﴾, that is, is it permissible, due to the smallness of his intellect, ﴿man﴾, that is, the one who is a servant, a created being, weak, powerless and needy, by what he sees in himself and in those of his kind.

When the impulse toward audacity was the absolute leaving alone (al-turk) without any restriction to a specific party, he said, constructing the verb in the passive: ﴿that he be left﴾ [that is, that his leaving be altogether] ﴿neglected (sudan)﴾, that is, left unattended, playing and heedless, not held accountable, not recompensed, and not presented before the Supreme King who created him so that He may ask him about his thankfulness for what He bestowed upon him. For that is incompatible with wisdom, since wisdom requires commanding good, forbidding evil, and recompensing each of them, and most of the wrongdoers and the wronged die without recompense; wisdom therefore necessarily requires resurrection for recompense.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 37:

Since man follows what is "in his nature" (fi tab'ihi) of deficiencies, he becomes heedless of that for which he was created, so his darknesses pile up upon him and he grows distant from knowledge of this, either through ignorance of wisdom or through ignorance of power. He (glory be to Him) showed him mercy by repeating the proof for the Return (al-ma'ad) through a matter that combines power and wisdom. That is because it is not permissible in the mind of any intelligent person that a Maker who makes a thing would leave it in neglect while He is wise or a judge, so how much more so for the Most Wise of the wise and the Most Judging of the judges. Thus He said, denouncing his assumption that He would leave him neglected (glory be to Him), despite His knowledge of His well-crafted works in him, establishing the conditions of his beginning, with which denying his return is not justified, because they are more indicative that nothing prevents it at all, omitting the nun of kawn (yakun) to inform that the matter in this great conclusion has become too narrow even for the smallest thing that can be dispensed with, out of dislike for the persistence of the one being admonished in what he was admonished for, so that destruction would befall him. It is also an indication of the lowliness of his origin and its contemptibility: ﴿Did he not used to be﴾, that is, man, ﴿a drop﴾, that is, something very insignificant, ﴿of semen emitted﴾, that is, water emitted from the loins of the man and the breastbones of the woman, intended and ordained by God for trial and testing; its example is the death that is the end, ﴿emitted﴾, that is, God caused man to be given the effort of expelling it by what He placed in him of desire, and gave him of the spirit that he hides in order to fulfill his need from it, to the extent that at the time of its pouring into the womb it is poured out from him without his choice, so much so that it is as if he has no act in it at all. For this reason He formed the verb in the passive voice, the one whose agent is not named.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 38:

Since the multiplying of that drop and its transformation was a great and wondrous matter, He indicated it with the particle of distance (thumma, "then"), which also conveys a delay in time. So He said: ﴿Then it became﴾, that is, a firmly established becoming, ﴿a clinging clot﴾, that is, pure red blood, extremely red and thick. ﴿Then He shaped﴾, that is, Glorified is He, decreed immediately after that its flesh, bones, sinews, and other essences and accidents, ﴿and proportioned﴾, that is, He turned from that into another creation, perfectly proportioned, an independent individual.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 75, verse 39:

Since their denial of the Resurrection (istib'ad) was either because they deemed it unlikely that power could restore the parts after they had been scattered, or because they deemed it unlikely that power could distinguish the dust of the dead from the dust of the earth after they had become mixed together, and since distinguishing the drop of semen into male and female was sufficient to refute both denials, He said: ﴿Then He made﴾, that is, by means of the drop (nutfah), ﴿from it﴾, that is, this gushing fluid, or the created and fashioned being, and they are one and the same thing, ﴿the two mates﴾, that is, the two counterparts, neither of which can be benefited from except by the other. Then He explained them with His words: ﴿the male and the female﴾. And they, as you know, differ in natural disposition and differ in the attributes of their organs, instruments and provisions. Just as He did not leave the drop until He turned it into a clot (\u2018alaqah), nor leave the clot until He turned it into a lump of flesh (mudghah), nor leave the lump of flesh until He turned it into bones, nor leave the bones until He turned them into another creation, up to the completion of the form, for the sake of the manifest wisdom, and He distinguished it into male and female, and it is [water], (p-118) the distinguishing of what is suitable from it for the male and what is suitable from it for the female is more severe and more hidden than distinguishing the dust of the dead from the dust of the earth. Likewise, the body is not left after its death until He restores it, then raises it, and so on to the end of that, for the sake of the complete inner wisdom, which is recompense, and the wisdom that is especially the property of the King.

When what has been established regarding the perfection of creation is that it does not allow for neglect or for the cessation of dispute, and it might be that someone hesitates because he supposes that re-creation after death is beyond God's power, He says, drawing attention to the completeness of power, affirming it, rebuking those who hesitate about it, and reproaching them, following from what was established about the power of re-creation by the evident proof of power in the origination: ﴿Is not He who does that﴾, that is, the Creator who fashioned, the supreme God, who has power over these formations and made these perfected works, none other being able to do any of them, and He intensified the negation, so He said: ﴿able to give life﴾, that is, of great power, ﴿to the dead﴾, that is, however He wills, at once or in successive times, ﴿so that He establishes the Resurrection﴾. Rather [wa -], by His might, His majesty, His greatness and His perfection, He is indeed over all things capable. He has returned at the end of the surah to its beginning with the most complete return, and it has joined with it in the most complete joining, so its meanings have been completed in the greatest completion, by gathering the bones and bringing about the standing up for the Day of Mutual Loss and the Crowding. May God help us in it [fihi -] according to the conclusion. Al-Baghawi related with his chain of narration, through the route of Abu Dawud, from a Bedouin, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you recites ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾ [al-Tin: 1] and reaches its end, ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin: 8], let him say: [bala -] 'Yes, and I am of those who bear witness to that.' And whoever recites ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1] and reaches His saying ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾, let him say 'Yes.' And whoever recites al-Mursalat and reaches ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 50], let him say: 'We believe in God.'" [wa -] It was related by al-Tirmidhi, and he said at the end of al-Qiyamah, "Able to give life to the dead": "Yes, by the might of our Lord." Al-Hafiz Nur al-Din al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id: Ahmad related, and in its chain are two men whom I do not know, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever recites: ﴿By the Mursalat, in custom, then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, and whoever recites: ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾, let him say: "And I am of those who bear witness to that", and whoever recites: ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾, let him say "Yes."'" And God is the Guide to what is right.
